title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:

More than half of organisations providing HIV care surveyed by International Planned Parenthood Federation said they had run out of stock at some point during past 12 months

Aid cuts have affected HIV drug and test supplies across the world, with some providers reporting they are out of stock of key medicines, according to a survey of 40 countries.

Organisations providing HIV care revealed that more than half (55%) had run out of stock within the past year, with a critical scarcity of HIV tests and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – a prescription medicine that people take to reduce the risk of getting HIV.

🔭 ✏️

Every new fossil fuel project that comes online will add more climate-warming carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions into our atmosphere. But just reporting how many tonnes (metric tons) of CO2 a new coal or gas facility will produce can still be abstract. 

What does it really mean, for example, that a single coal mine in Australia will generate an estimated 4.7 billion tonnes of emissions over its lifetime? How will those emissions actually, tangibly impact the world and its inhabitants?

A new open-source tool quantifies that impact, translating tonnes of CO2 emissions into measurable damages—like the number of excess heat deaths in Europe, the cost of crop production loss, or how many more coral reef colonies will succumb to bleaching. 

Called the Carbon Impacts Tracer, the tool was created by climate experts at Australia National University and the University of New South Wales, as well as the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century and the Lethal Humidity Global Council.

The tracer shows how much damage emissions will cause across eight categories:

  • excess deaths in Europe
  • Great Barrier Reef coral loss
  • crop production loss; glacier loss
  • the loss of labor hours
  • how many more people will be exposed to heat stress
  • additional people in poverty
  • “human climate niche,” which refers to the narrow range of temperatures in which humans have historically lived

For example, take that Australian coal mine: the Carmichael coal project.

Select it from a list of scenarios in the Carbon Impacts Tracer, and the tool can tell you that those 4.7 billion tonnes of emissions would cause an estimated 2,628 additional heat-related deaths in Europe. Or those emissions could be quantified as a crop loss equivalent to the annual food supply for 1.62 million people. Or 87.4 million additional coral colonies lost per bleaching event. Or 248,000 more people tipped into extreme poverty. Or 1.9 million people left outside of the human climate niche. 

Though the tool includes multiple Australian projects that users can preselect, it also features a couple of international examples, such as the Bay Du Nord Project, an offshore oil development off the coast of Canada. 

Brought to you by attribution science

The tracer includes company-level scenarios for fossil fuel giants like BP, ExxonMobil, and Shell. It also allows users to enter a custom emissions amount anywhere between 1 million and 10 billion metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent. 

We know that every tonne of carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere increases global warming, which amplifies climate impacts like heat waves, floods, glacier melt, and so on.

But historically, it’s been difficult to say how much damage a certain amount of emissions or a specific fossil fuel project will actually cause. Researchers have been expanding this field, known as attribution science, which helps specify just how big a role climate change plays in specific instances of extreme weather or natural disasters.

By turning emissions into specific heat-related deaths or crop loss figures, the tool’s creators say that it will make both the fossil fuel companies and governments that approve these projects “accountable for the damage they will do.”

“For decades, fossil fuel producers have been able to extract oil, gas, and coal, and emit pollution to the atmosphere with virtual impunity—even as climate change worsens and damages mount,” the creators wrote in a piece published by the University of New South Wales.

“But we are entering a new era of accountability,” they continue. “Now that climate attribution science has come of age, it’s no longer possible to hide behind the argument that a new gas field is just a drop in the ocean. We can now see just how much damage that drop will do to the climate, nature—and to us.”

items.title: [Fast Company] Grindr is spending $250M to signal that it’s getting serious about LGBTQ+ healthcare
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Grindr is expanding its footprint in LGBTQ-focused healthcare with its first major acquisition. The dating app is paying $250 million for health startup Freddie, with the aim of fully integrating Freddie’s HIV-prevention telehealth and pharmacy capabilities into a broader Grindr Health offering.

The launch of Grindr Health builds on the company’s telehealth business Woodwork, which launched in 2025 to connect users with medication for weight loss and erectile dysfunction. As of Wednesday, when the acquisition was announced, users can access features from both Freddie and Woodwork through a Grindr Health portal in the app.

Grindr CEO George Arison has long credited the app with helping to make HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) more mainstream. The preventive medication is 99% effective at reducing the sexual transmission of the virus.

As of 2025, the United States reached a record high of more than 644,000 PrEP users, a 10% increase from 2024. But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that 2.2 million Americans could benefit from PrEP—meaning the medicine is still reaching less than a third of its potential users in the country, and there’s a lot of room for Grindr’s new business to grow.

“It’s a situation where everybody that can be on this drug should be on this drug, because it’s healthier for them and healthier for people that they meet,” Arison tells Fast Company. “To us, [PrEP access] seems like a natural opportunity and a win-win, to both build a great business as well as do something really important for public health,” he says.

Adding a pharmacy to the gayborhood

Arison says contracting HIV is “the one thing that all gay men are scared of,” suggesting that taking PrEP should be common sense for the app’s users. But mirroring broader U.S. statistics, Grindr reports that only 400,000 of its millions of American users identify as being on PrEP.

“If we achieve the same market share in the U.S. on PrEP that Freddie has in Canada . . . that will mean [an additional] 200,000 people on PrEP, and that will mean about 5,000 people not getting HIV a year,” Arison adds. With the most recent CDC findings showing an estimated 31,800 new HIV infections in the U.S. per year, that means Grindr could play a significant role in driving down HIV infections nationwide.

Adding in more healthcare to complement Woodwork—which initially offered erectile dysfuynction medication and has since expanded to include GLP-1s—is part of Arison’s effort to make users (and investors) see Grindr as a “global gayborhood,” not just a place for hookups. The company has been leveraging AI to build new features that improve the user experience and offer specific insights about people that users might want to connect with.

“Don’t think of Grindr as a dating product. Think of Grindr as a social network that has a very unique pulse on the user base,” he says. “Obviously, we needed to prove to everyone that that’s what we were. This is just a logical next step in that direction.”

Good for health, good for business

As Arison has been expanding his vision for Grindr beyond just connecting people, he’s also been improving the company’s revenue and subscriber base.

In the second quarter of 2026, Grindr reported a revenue of $138 million, a 33% year-over-year increase. Meanwhile, the app’s paying user base continues to grow, with a current 1.4 million users paying for Grindr features including its XTRA and Unlimited subscription tiers, up 16% from last year.

Researchers at Morgan Stanley noted the clear rationale for Grindr’s acquisition of Freddie, pointing to the app’s earlier telehealth success through Woodwork. And even before that launch, Grindr successfully connected more than 2 million users with mpox vaccines in 2022.

The analysts also highlighted Freddie’s strong earning potential for Grindr. The telehealth platform has higher gross margins than its peers, as Freddie generates revenue from referral fees to entities receiving federal discounts through the U.S.’s 340B Drug Pricing Program.

With each active patient estimated to generate $4,800 in revenue for a full year, Arison sees the acquisition as a financial no-brainer as well. If the company achieves it’s baseline goal of 50,000 Grindr users getting PrEP through the app, it would generate $240 million in revenue annually.

Moving forward, Arison says the acquisition sets the brand up “for a much broader Grindr Health vision.” One example? Putting users in touch with health professionals who are part of or experts on LGTBQ+ health.

“I talk to so many people—myself included, honestly—who want a gay doctor and cannot get a gay doctor,” Arison says. “Over time, we can be in a place where we’re giving way more capability to our users to find gay doctors, and be able to connect with them virtually for their other healthcare needs.”
